column4: At the resurrection, people follow the caller without deviation, their voices are humbled before the Most Merciful, and only a whisper is heard; this stages the fear-driven hush named in the section.
In the garden they hear no لَغْوًا, only peace, directly matching 88:11's exclusion of لَاغِيَةً and the section's question of what sound replaces silence.
The garden dwellers hear neither idle speech nor sinful words, spelling out the kind of utterance absent from the soundscape of 88:11.
The next ayah supplies the positive sound: only words of peace are heard, giving a fitting utterance in place of harmful talk.
The garden has neither laghw nor falsehood to be heard, extending the section's protected silence from ugly speech to lying.
This garden scene excludes both idle and sin-inducing speech, another precise formulation of what 88:11's لا تسمع concerns.
Those given Scripture turn away when they hear اللغو and answer with peace; the passage links hearing to refusing empty or abusive talk.
After successive peoples reject their messengers, God says He made them أحاديث; they become the cautionary reports that a hearer may one day be.
After the people of Saba' complain and are scattered, God says He made them أحاديث, directly illustrating the section's secondary sense of people turned into exemplary reports.
وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ repeats the section's opening “has the report come to you?” and then unfolds Moses' story.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ repeats the report-arrival formula and opens the account of Abraham's honored guests.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ الْجُنُودِ repeats the same report-arrival opening; 85:18 then identifies the armies with Pharaoh and Thamud.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ uses the same “has Moses' report come to you?” opening as 88:1, then begins his story.
God says He relates the best of stories to the Prophet through this revealed Qur'an; it makes explicit the section's point that a hadith reaches people through revelation as well as hearing.
The Prophet is told, “We relate to you news of what has passed,” and is given a reminder, joining narrated report to remembrance as the section does.
Joseph's and the other messengers' stories contain a lesson, and the Qur'an is not an invented hadith; the ayah joins narrative, report, and the hearer's admonition.
The Qur'an itself is called أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ; its repeated recitation moves reverent listeners from shivering to softened hearts and remembrance.
After God's signs are recited, the ayah asks what حديث people will believe in after God and His signs, treating revelation as the decisive report.
After the warnings in the surah, the question فَبِأَيِّ حَدِيثٍ بَعْدَهُ يُؤْمِنُونَ makes the Qur'anic message itself the report whose hearing calls for belief.
When the Qur'an is recited, listeners are told to listen and be silent so that they may receive mercy, a direct command for attentive hearing.
The praised servants listen to speech and follow its best; the ayah shows سماع as understanding and choosing a response, not merely catching sound.
The believers say they heard a caller summoning them to faith and then believed, carrying the section's path from an arriving utterance to a listener's response.
The ark's rescue is made a reminder, the ayah says, for an ear that retains it; it pictures the hearer holding a report as remembrance.
The account is called a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while present, explicitly joining remembrance to attentive listening.
In the battle passage some say “we hear” while in fact not hearing; it exposes the gap between catching words and heeding them that the section's سماع sense allows.
When called to God's and the Messenger's judgment, believers answer “we hear and obey”; this puts the section's obedience-sense of hearing into a concrete response.
The people of the Fire regret that they did not listen or reason; the ayah makes failed hearing and understanding consequential, as the section's warning-report implies.
On the Day of the Spirit and angels standing in rows, none speaks except by the Merciful's permission and with a right word; it gives a boundary to the judgment-day hush.
“Remind, if the reminder benefits” closely parallels 88:21's command فَذَكِّرْ and its account of the Prophet as reminder-bearer.
The command “remind, for the reminder benefits believers” states the purpose of the speech 88:21 assigns to the Prophet.
The Prophet is told to remind by the Qur'an whoever fears God's threat, specifying the report used by the reminder in 88:21.
The Qur'an is called a reminder, directly naming what the Prophet's فَذَكِّرْ in 88:21 carries.
Whoever wills may take heed of that reminder; the ayah supplies the listener's side of 88:21's reminder exchange.
The revelation is called a reminder, connecting the incoming report with the reminder the Prophet is then told to deliver.
Whoever wills may remember it, showing the listener's choice in response to the reminder.
After Noah's people are warned, the refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance and asks who will remember; it ties a delivered warning to its hearer.
The same refrain follows the warning to 'Ad, repeating the link between recited admonition and a hearer's remembering.
After Thamud's destruction, the same refrain makes the account itself an accessible reminder for its audience.
After Lot's people are warned and punished, the refrain again asks who will remember the delivered account.
The Prophet's duty is only to convey while the reckoning belongs to God; it defines the messenger's report-bearing role alongside the final accounting in the surah.

The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ نَبَأُ الْخَصْمِ introduces the litigants climbing into David's chamber; its arrival-of-news formula opens a staged account like the section's question, using nabāʾ rather than hadith.
The surah opens by asking about the great news, then identifies the disputed subject; it makes the coming judgment a report people are already discussing.
The Prophet is told that the messengers' accounts are recited to steady him and serve as reminder and admonition for believers, a concrete purpose for received stories.
At Joseph's story's close, the ayah calls it news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet, who was not present at the brothers' plotting; it exemplifies a report arriving by revelation.
Mary's guardianship is called news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet though he was not present; the ayah grounds the section's revelation route for a report.
Asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, the Prophet is told to recite a remembrance of him, turning a question into a spoken account as in the section's opening frame.
The listeners are challenged about this hadith and their response of laughter rather than tears, a specific example of hearing revelation without its intended response.
Some people acquire لَهْوَ الْحَدِيثِ to divert others from God's path; this is speech used to distract, set against the section's report that calls its hearer to remembrance.
A new reminder from their Lord reaches the people, yet they listen while playing and their hearts are distracted; it reverses the attentive reception sought by 88:21.
Whenever a new reminder comes from the Merciful, the rejecters turn away; the incoming word is present but refused, unlike the hearer who carries it onward.
Believers are commanded to obey God and the Messenger and not turn away while they hear; the ayah makes hearing a call to obedience.
The covenant recalls the believers' answer “we hear and obey”; it gives a concrete instance of hearing joined to submission.
The believers answer revelation with “we hear and obey,” showing the section's obedience-sense of سماع in response to the scripture.
The ayah reports people saying “we hear and disobey” while twisting words; it makes explicit the difference between hearing sound and accepting what is heard.
When reminded of their Lord's signs, the servants do not fall on them deaf and blind; it depicts receptive hearing rather than the refusal described elsewhere.
Hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, adding accountability to the section's picture of someone who receives a report by ear.
When the Most Merciful's verses are recited to earlier prophets, they fall prostrate and weep; the ayah shows an audible reminder moving its hearers to response.
Those who lower their voices near God's Messenger have hearts tested for piety; this is reverent, deliberate lowering of sound, unlike the fear-hushed voices of the Judgment scene.
The successful believers turn away from اللغو, extending the section's concern with speech that has no place in a purified life.
When the servants of the Merciful are addressed harshly by the ignorant, they answer with peace; it shows peace replacing an ugly exchange.
The servants of the Merciful pass by laghw with dignity rather than joining it, an earthly counterpart to the garden's absence of such speech.
In the Garden their prayer is praise, their greeting is peace, and their final words are praise; the ayah names the good speech replacing harmful talk.
The garden's greeting is “Peace,” a word from a merciful Lord, giving a specific positive utterance where 88:11 says no ugly speech is heard.
Angels greet the patient in the Garden with peace; it is another concrete garden utterance consistent with the section's replacement of laghw by salutations.
The people admitted to the gardens have peace as their greeting there, naming the speech that replaces idle or foul talk.
The Prophet's household is told to remember what is recited in their homes of God's signs and wisdom, joining recitation to remembrance as the section's definition does.
The passage says the number of the Fire's guardians is a trial and reminder for believers and scripture readers; it shows a disturbing report serving admonition.
When people turn away, the Prophet is told he was not sent as their keeper and has only to convey; it marks the boundary of the reminder's messenger, as 88:21-22 does.
When mockers engage God's signs, the Prophet must leave them until they enter another حديث; the boundary protects revelation from degrading discourse.
When God's verses are denied and mocked, believers must leave until the group takes up another حديث; this sets a boundary around what speech they attend.
The rejecters say not to listen to the Qur'an and to make laghw over it; their deliberate cacophony reverses the attentive, purified hearing of the section.
The condemned are told “be despised therein and do not speak to Me”; this punitive silence contrasts with the garden's freedom from harmful speech.
